memorial_note: Bismarck is a war grave. Roughly 2,100 of her crew of 2,221 died when she sank on 27 May 1941; only around 114 were rescued from the freezing North Atlantic. Please explore her the way you would any grave: look and learn, and leave her exactly as she lies. This game has no salvage, collection or loot of any kind, anywhere.

entries.title: Bismarck: the last battle
paragraphs: Bismarck was one of the largest battleships ever built by Germany, commissioned in August 1940. In May 1941 she sailed into the North Atlantic with the heavy cruiser Prinz Eugen on Operation Rheinubung, a commerce raid intended to disrupt Allied shipping. The Royal Navy intercepted her, opening a three-day pursuit that became one of the most famous naval actions of the Second World War.

On 24 May 1941, at the Battle of the Denmark Strait, Bismarck and Prinz Eugen engaged HMS Hood and HMS Prince of Wales. Hood was destroyed in minutes, with all but three of her 1,419 crew lost; Bismarck took damage that forced her to abandon the raid and head for occupied France for repairs. Swordfish torpedo bombers from HMS Victorious and, on 26 May, from HMS Ark Royal found and struck her; a torpedo hit near the stern jammed her rudders, leaving her unable to steer clear of the pursuing British fleet. On the morning of 27 May, HMS King George V and HMS Rodney closed in and bombarded her for almost two hours. With the ship ablaze, listing, and unable to fight back, her crew opened the sea cocks and detonated scuttling charges; she sank, stern-first, at roughly 10:40. Of her crew of 2,221, only around 114 were rescued -- most by HMS Dorsetshire and HMS Maori, who broke off the rescue early on report of a U-boat sighting.

The wreck was found on 8 June 1989 by an expedition led by Robert Ballard, the oceanographer who had located Titanic four years earlier. It has since been surveyed several more times, most extensively by Magellan's 2019 digital-twin project led by naval historian Parks Stephenson.

What you see here: the seabed is real bathymetry, but this part of the North Atlantic has no dedicated multibeam survey of the wreck site, so it falls back to a coarser global fill -- far too coarse to show a 251 m hull. The ship is built from published photographs, survey reports and the ship's known dimensions, placed at the H.M.S. Hood Association's 2001 expedition fix (48.15N, 16.117W), the most specific sourced coordinate found among several published figures.

facts.label: Protection
facts.value: war grave; treated as such by every expedition

entries.title: Upright on the seamount
paragraphs: Bismarck rests upright on the south-eastern flank of a large, extinct undersea volcano, roughly halfway down its slope. Survey teams describe the hull as in surprisingly good condition for its age and the violence of its final battle: essentially intact, resting embedded in mud, with only a small section of the stern reported broken away at one survey (kbismarck.com). This account sits in tension with data/landmarks.json's own summary, which describes the bow as separated from the main hull -- we found no single authoritative survey report reconciling the two claims, so both are noted here rather than one silently dropped (see sources.md).

When the turrets tore loose and struck the seamount, the impact triggered a small landslide that carried the settling hull a further distance down the slope before it came to rest -- published accounts put the debris trail at around a kilometre. Bismarck's own crew scuttled her as the British bombardment closed in, and cumulative shell and torpedo damage almost certainly would have sunk her regardless; historians still debate how much each cause contributed (see the battle-damage entry).

The block you see here uses the ship's published length and beam. No source found gives a precise hull height above the seabed or the ship's actual compass heading. It is placed at the H.M.S. Hood Association's 2001 expedition fix, the most specific sourced coordinate found; this tile's own terrain there reads roughly 4,220 m, shallower than the 4,790-4,791 m commonly published for the wreck's final resting depth, because the point sits higher on the seamount's flank than the hull's reported final position after its landslide.

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: upright, largely intact (accounts vary on the bow/stern)

facts.label: Survey
facts.value: Ballard 1989; multiple later expeditions, most recently Magellan (2019)

sources.title: The Wreck of the Bismarck — kbismarck.com

entries.title: The main gun turrets
paragraphs: Bismarck's four main-battery turrets, Anton, Bruno, Caesar and Dora, each carrying a pair of 38 cm guns, were bolted from below rather than fixed rigidly to the hull. As the ship rolled and sank, they broke free of their barbettes and fell separately, striking the seamount slope before the hull itself came to rest.

Ballard's 1989 team located only one turret, lying upside-down and half-buried in sediment, and could not find the other three. Later, more thorough surveys -- notably Magellan's 2019 digital-twin project -- mapped a fuller debris field across the slope, including turrets in a roughly straight line, one pushed out of alignment as the hull slid past it.

facts.label: Turrets
facts.value: Anton, Bruno, Caesar, Dora — 4 x twin 38 cm

sources.title: Bismarck Wreck: Main Gun Barrels — Naval History Forums (kbismarck.org)

entries.title: Shellfire, torpedoes, or scuttling?
paragraphs: By the morning of 27 May 1941, Bismarck could no longer steer or fight back effectively: a torpedo hit near the stern two days earlier had jammed her rudders, and HMS King George V and HMS Rodney closed to point-blank range and battered her for nearly two hours. With the ship ablaze and listing heavily, her crew opened the sea cocks and set off scuttling charges below decks, and she went down stern-first around 10:40.

Exactly what finally sank her has been debated by historians and naval architects for decades: British gunners and a final torpedo strike from HMS Dorsetshire certainly inflicted catastrophic damage, but German survivors maintained the scuttling charges were what actually sent her under. Most researchers today conclude both contributed -- the ship was doomed by battle damage regardless, and the scuttling likely hastened an outcome already underway.
This marker is placed near the hull to represent that question rather than a single surveyed feature; the hull's true damage pattern is not modelled in detail here.

facts.label: Final bombardment
facts.value: 27 May, HMS King George V and HMS Rodney

facts.label: Cause
facts.value: debated: battle damage, scuttling, or both

entries.title: An extinct undersea volcano
paragraphs: Bismarck lies on the flank of a large, extinct seamount in the eastern North Atlantic. This tile's own terrain shows a broad, undulating slope: it shoals from about 4,219 m at the hull to roughly 4,182 m some 500 m up-slope to the north-east, and continues up toward the tile's shallowest point (a summit) at about 4,024 m roughly 3 km further along the same line.

That is real, if coarse, bathymetry -- but it is not a survey of the wreck site itself, and the depth here (around 4,220 m) reads noticeably shallower than the 4,790-4,791 m commonly published for the wreck: the sourced coordinate used marks the general vicinity of the wreck, not necessarily the exact point the hull settled at after sliding downslope. Published accounts describe a much steeper slope near the actual wreck, around 14.5 degrees, and a roughly 1 km debris trail down it, formed when the falling turrets triggered a small landslide that carried the settling hull further downhill. This tile's grid comes from a coarser global (GEBCO-derived) fill rather than a dedicated multibeam survey of the site, so it cannot resolve that trail, the true slope angle, or the exact depth; what you can scan here is genuine terrain, smoothed well below the scale of the wreck.

facts.label: Published wreck depth
facts.value: 4,790-4,791 m (deeper than this tile reads here)

facts.label: Data source
facts.value: GMRT Synthesis (coarse fill here, not a dedicated survey)

sources.title: Global Multi-Resolution Topography (GMRT) Synthesis — Ryan et al. 2009, doi:10.1029/2008GC002332

entries.title: A war grave
paragraphs: Bismarck went down with roughly 2,100 of the 2,221 men aboard her. HMS Dorsetshire and HMS Maori pulled about 110 survivors from the freezing water before breaking off, on the report of a possible U-boat; a few more were later picked up by a German weather ship and U-boat. It remains one of the largest single losses of life in the Battle of the Atlantic.

Every expedition to the wreck, from Ballard's in 1989 onward, has treated the site as a war grave: no recovery of remains or artefacts, cameras and sensors only. This game follows the same principle at every site it depicts, war grave or not -- there is no salvage, collection or loot of any kind.

facts.label: Status
facts.value: treated as a war grave by every expedition
